This 345-million-year-old fossil had scientists fooled for decades

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (886 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A small fossil discovered in Scotland and regarded for nearly three decades as one of the earliest known reptiles has turned out to be a very different kind of prehistoric animal.
  • Industry observers note that the 345-million-year-old fossil, discovered in 1984, belongs to a species called Westlothiana lizziae.
  • It has been revealed that although the fossil's distorted condition made its anatomy difficult to interpret, researchers widely regarded it as the earliest known amniote adapted to life on land.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A small fossil discovered in Scotland and regarded for nearly three decades as one of the earliest known reptiles has turned out to be a very different kind of prehistoric animal. Latest research published in Nature is challenging its long-established place in evolutionary history. The study was led by scientists at the American Museum of Natural History and the University of Oxford, working in collaboration with the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility.

Industry observers note that the 345-million-year-old fossil, discovered in 1984, belongs to a species called Westlothiana lizziae. Nicknamed "Lizzie" because of its resemblance to a lizard, the specimen consists of a nearly complete skeleton preserved in two crushed slabs of rock. Early descriptions relied largely on anatomical features visible at the surface, including four limbs with fingers and toes that appeared to have claw-like tips. These characteristics distinguished Westlothiana from many other animals living at the time, whose limbs more closely resembled fins.

It has been revealed that although the fossil's distorted condition made its anatomy difficult to interpret, researchers widely regarded it as the earliest known amniote adapted to life on land. Amniotes are a major group of vertebrates that includes reptiles, birds, and mammals. Following its scientific description in 1990, Westlothiana became an important reference point for researchers investigating when and how these animals first evolved.

"Lizzie has been an icon for the early evolution of amniotes for decades," mentioned Xavier Jenkins, a postdoctoral fellow in the Museum's Division of Paleontology and co-lead author of the study. "But when we were finally able to see inside the fossil, we found an animal that looked very different from what we expected.".

Advanced X-Ray Scans Reveal Lizzie's True Identity.

Using powerful X-ray imaging technology at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility in Grenoble, France, the scientists peered beneath the surface of the rock and reconstructed previously inaccessible parts of the animal's anatomy.

What they discovered was strikingly different from the anatomy expected in an early reptile. Lizzie possessed a primitive skull, internal gills containing bone, and a mouth resembling that of a fish, complete with thousands of tiny teeth. Together, these features rule out its previously proposed position within the evolutionary lineage leading to reptiles. Instead of living primarily on land, Westlothiana appears to have been an aquatic or amphibious animal.

Sources indicate that "The surprisingly primitive features of the skull show us that Lizzie was not only not a reptile but belonged to a much more ancient lineage. It turns out looks can be deceiving, and Lizzie lived a completely different lifestyle than we previously thought," noted Ben Igielman, co-lead author of the study, who started this research during his graduate work at the University of Oxford.

Reptile-Like Features Evolved in Aquatic Ancestors.

The discovery also changes how scientists understand the origins of several anatomical features traditionally associated with vertebrates adapted to terrestrial environments.

Researchers now believe that characteristics such as claws and the arrangement of five digits on each hand and foot, a pattern familiar in reptiles and mammals, had already emerged in earlier animals that were still closely associated with water. These creatures belonged to the evolutionary lineage leading to tetrapods, the broader group of four-limbed vertebrates that encompasses both amphibians and amniotes.

Recent findings suggest that "This is a big surprise," stated study co-author Roger Benson, the Museum's Macaulay Curator of Paleontology. "It demonstrates that, although we think of amphibians as being more 'primitive' than reptiles today, some of the traits of reptiles were already there in the ancestor of both amphibians and reptiles.".

Ancient Footprints May Tell a Different Story.

The findings could also have notable implications for the interpretation of prehistoric fossil tracks. Recently discovered trackways have been used as evidence that amniotes first appeared during the Devonian Period, more than 359 million years ago.

According to recent reports, these ancient impressions record the movements of a four-limbed animal with apparently clawed digits. However, if distant relatives of tetrapods such as Westlothiana also possessed claws, such footprints are no longer sufficient on their own to identify the animals that left them as amniotes.

Some trackways previously attributed to early amniotes may instead have been left by more ancient, amphibious creatures belonging to the evolutionary lineage of tetrapods.

"The broader lesson is that terrestrial-looking traits, such as a reptile-like foot, a weight-bearing forelimb, and claw-like phalanges were not unique features of tetrapods, but rather accumulated piecemeal in their close relatives, in animals that were still living in and out of the water," Jenkins remarked.

Additional contributors to the study include Jason Head from the University of Cambridge, Vincent Fernandez from the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility, Lucy Roberts from the Natural History Museum, London, and Timothy Smithson from the University Museum of Zoology Cambridge.

The research received funding from the National Science Foundation (grant number EAR-PF 2518154), the National Environment Research Council (grant numbers NE/S000739/1, NE/W007576/1, and NE/L002507/1), and the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (grant number BB/X014819/1).

#151739. Breaking: Welcome to the Repair Café, Where Neighbors Fight Throwaway Culture

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1561 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Welcome to the Repair Café, Where Neighbors Fight Throwaway Culture

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1561 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story originally appeared on Grist and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
  • In a recent development, on an unusually cool and rainy Saturday morning in Decatur, Georgia, dozens of people filed into a warehouse at the back of a church parking lot, their arms full of what a less hopeful group might call junk.
  • That’s how Lilly Pettus ended up shoulder to shoulder with three strangers, their hands all pressing together the pieces of her family’s cracked dining room chair as wood glue hardened and a volunteer tightened a clamp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story originally appeared on Grist and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

In a recent development, on an unusually cool and rainy Saturday morning in Decatur, Georgia, dozens of people filed into a warehouse at the back of a church parking lot, their arms full of what a less hopeful group might call junk. Some carried broken lamps, glitching electronics, or cracked furniture. Others walked in with toolboxes, multimeters for testing electric currents, and cans of WD-40. Beneath extension cords dangling from the rafters, they sorted themselves into smaller groups: the volunteer electricians, tailors, luthiers, carpenters, and at least one cutler (knife sharpener), commandeering nearby worktables and passersby as needed.

That’s how Lilly Pettus ended up shoulder to shoulder with three strangers, their hands all pressing together the pieces of her family’s cracked dining room chair as wood glue hardened and a volunteer tightened a clamp.

“This is so interesting,” a giddy Pettus said, inspecting for the first time the joints, one of them broken, that held together the chair she’d owned for decades. “You never even know how furniture is put together.”.

This is Decatur’s semi-regular repair café, one of a few hundred meetings like it across the United States. More Americans than ever are turning to these community gatherings to fix what they already own, resisting the influence of companies that sell everything from hiking boots to smartphones and hot water boilers and that push for replacement over repair. One consequence of this throwaway economy is an increase in greenhouse gas emissions from manufacturing that threatens to intensify climate change.

It has been revealed that yet, organizers and volunteers consider repair cafés to be more than a relatively small climate solution. As inflation rises and wages stagnate, the meetups connect people to a movement with the ambitious goal of changing the fundamentals of America’s consumer economy.

At the Decatur repair café, volunteers, wearing green shirts with “I can probably fix that” printed on the back, offered their skills free of charge as patrons observed. A young father of a toddler and squirmy baby watched as a volunteer replaced a switch on a favorite mid-century modern lamp worn out by the older child’s repeated clicking. Murmurs of excitement rippled around the building as the acrid smell of a spot welding project wafted through.

Pettus’ broken chair held in its wood her family’s story. Soon after she and her husband were married in 1996, they began a search for a dining room set. Pettus wanted the chairs to be comfortable for her entire family, but one of her brothers is nearly 7 feet tall, and another just a few inches shorter. “We are not a tiny family,” Pettus said. “We are a massive family.”.

It has been revealed that pettus also thought of one of her children who’d interned at the Environmental Protection Agency and shared his concerns with Pettus about pollution and climate change. Then, after months of the broken chair cluttering the family’s house, Pettus was running Saturday morning errands when she passed the Decatur repair café. She drove the half-mile home to grab the chair and decided to give it a second chance.

“When a product breaks and you have to throw it away, it’s very lonely,” said Martine Postma, director of Repair Café International, a Netherlands-based network of 4,000 cafés. “ It’s easier to just go on the internet and order a newly introduced item which will come to your doorstep in 24 hours, but that’s also a very lonely, disconnected activity.”.

Postma, a former journalist with the demeanor of an unflappable librarian, founded her organization in 2010 after the birth of her second child magnified her fears about the planet’s future. “Markets are flooded with trash—with cheap products that we don’t need and that do not work,” Postma stated. “They break, and they contribute nothing to our well-being. They just contribute waste.”.

Repair cafés appear to be inspiring people to use their stuff longer. In 2025, they prevented nearly 2 million pounds of waste—the equivalent of more than 100 fully loaded Boeing 747 aircraft—according to Repair Café International, and reduced greenhouse gas emissions equivalent to the average consumption of about 1,000 Dutch families.

Industry observers note that postma, Pettus, and millions of others often smack into obstacles when they try to fix their own stuff. Broken products are increasingly difficult to repair, according to a report from the Federal Trade Commission titled “Nixing the Fix.” The report details how Americans are incentivized to “replace products before the end of their useful lives” by companies that decide to make repairs less safe, limit the availability of parts, lock software and firmware, or even “disparage” independent repair.

Sources indicate that in 2023, California, Colorado, Minnesota, and Fresh York passed “right to repair” legislation meant to encourage repair over replacement. A year later the European Union passed a similar directive. Postma and other organizers consider the cafés a natural place for activism to push for right-to-repair measures, although Postma hopes for more sweeping changes in Europe, like a tax on raw materials. She argued it would limit emissions and bolster repair shops, even if it increases the cost of products.

Sources indicate that “ I feel for the objects around me. I feel sorry for them if they’re broken,” she mentioned. “I want to make repairing a normal thing in everyday life once more.”.

Industry observers note that according to Postma, repairing goods is more common in relatively poor countries where replacing them can be especially difficult and expensive. It’s in wealthy countries that repair cafés are thriving, but they’re not at all uniform. Each reflects the surrounding area and its socioeconomics.

On a Sunday afternoon in the Collier Heights neighborhood of Atlanta, volunteers brought most of their own tools to the basement of a building owned by a Seventh-Day Adventist Church, setting them on white plastic folding tables atop a light pink carpet. The café looked much different from the one a 30-minute drive across the city in Decatur. The median annual household income in the mostly Black Collier Heights neighborhood is roughly $40,000 lower than in Decatur. Many people who brought items wanted them fixed less for sentimental reason, and more so they could keep using them.

It has been revealed that gale Pines walked in with a red air fryer that had stopped working after they used it to dehydrate ginger. When their oven ran, Pines said, it heated the entire kitchen. So, while in nursing school, they cooked many of their evening meals in the air fryer, most often chicken nuggets and fries.

Pines recently graduated but had trouble finding a job and couldn’t afford to buy a new $100 air fryer. “It’s just hard to exist,” Pines remarked. “I don’t really have a very big support network outside of my friends.”.

In a recent development, one of Pines’ housemates told them about Collier Heights’ repair café. They keep a bag of broken electronics in the garage that they’d prefer not to send to a landfill. “Being in the height of climate collapse we can’t just keep buying latest stuff all the time, both for the economy and for our material scarcity,” Pines said.

Recent findings suggest that when a volunteer at the Collier Heights repair café opened up the air fryer, they quickly discovered the problem: a bad capacitor. Another volunteer had brought a replacement part, and the two of them made the fix as Pines watched, impressed, but unable to follow the relatively complex repair. Pines felt OK that they hadn’t learned how to fix the air fryer themself.

“ To just be around people that want to help other people with the skills that they have, that’s value that is really important to me and something that I try to do as well,” Pines said. “If somebody in my community has a question about their medication or something and can’t afford to go to the doctor, I’m happy to answer any questions that people have.”.

Another volunteer, Lew Lefton, said he thought that the satisfaction humans draw from making and fixing things has largely been lost, but apocalyptic threats like climate change and artificial intelligence have driven many people toward rediscovering more basic, human skills that are key to survival. People who come to a repair café have a different way to view the future, according to Lefton, especially if they learn something or volunteer themselves. “If the world ends,” he said, “at least I’ll know how to fix a motor.”.

Back in Decatur, Pettus left the repair café with a newly sturdy chair. A screw and some glue fixed the crack around the joint, but the chair still needed upholstery work. Someone Pettus met at the café, who had provided one of the sets of hands that held her chair together as the glue set, advised her on where to buy fabric. Pettus thought she might bring the chair back to the repair café for help reupholstering its seat cushion.

Industry observers note that “The beauty of it,” Pettus said, “was that I actually was able to learn more about the chair. It was a great experience to know that—I’m not gonna say I birthed it, I of course did not—but I actually had something to do with helping to get it put back together.”.

#151736. These bizarre prehistoric mammals may have been misunderstood for 150 years

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1359 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

These bizarre prehistoric mammals may have been misunderstood for 150 years

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1359 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For generations, paleontologists have regarded an extinct group of giant mammals known as uintatheres as a textbook example of sexual dimorphism, the physical differences between males and females of the same species.
  • Recognizable by their enormous bodies, prominent horns, and oversized canine teeth, uintatheres first appeared approximately 58 million years ago, less than 10 million years after an asteroid wiped out the dinosaurs.
  • However, upcoming research from the University of Kansas published in PLOS One suggests that the physical differences between male and female uintatheres may have been considerably less pronounced than scientists have long assumed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For generations, paleontologists have regarded an extinct group of giant mammals known as uintatheres as a textbook example of sexual dimorphism, the physical differences between males and females of the same species.

Recognizable by their enormous bodies, prominent horns, and oversized canine teeth, uintatheres first appeared approximately 58 million years ago, less than 10 million years after an asteroid wiped out the dinosaurs. These unusual mammals persisted for roughly 20 million years.

However, upcoming research from the University of Kansas published in PLOS One suggests that the physical differences between male and female uintatheres may have been considerably less pronounced than scientists have long assumed.

"Males have been interpreted as being much larger and possessing far more dramatic cranial features than females," said study author Kevin Mulcahy, doctoral student at the KU Biodiversity Institute & Natural History Museum.

A Broken Fossil Tooth Leads to an Unexpected Discovery.

The investigation began when Mulcahy and his doctoral adviser, K. Christopher Beard, senior curator at the institute, attempted to identify a broken upper molar recovered during fieldwork in Montana. The researchers suspected the tooth belonged to a uintathere but needed additional fossil specimens to confirm its identity.

"We had a research visit at the American Museum of Natural History in Latest York, where our main goal was just to compare that tooth to teeth from other uintatheres and figure out what type of animal we had," Mulcahy noted. "They have this big collection -- entire shelves occupied with these skulls, and each one of them is almost a meter long. These are famous specimens that are in the literature, and I was originally just looking at them to compare their teeth, and I noticed a ton of variation in a way that didn't appear binary.".

Intrigued by the unexpected range of physical characteristics, Mulcahy began measuring the skulls in the museum's collection.

"I just, really hastily, with a ruler, gathered a bunch of measurements of the skulls while we were there," Mulcahy stated. "I started playing around with statistics, and there are ways you can look at different measurements to see if they're best fit by a classic unimodal distribution, or if you were to think you're dealing with something that exhibits strong sexual dimorphism, you'd see something with a bimodal distribution -- that there are two means, one for males and one for females.".

Ancient Skulls Challenge a Classic Example of Sexual Dimorphism.

If males and females differed as dramatically as paleontologists had suggested, the skull measurements would be expected to cluster into two relatively distinct groups. Instead, Mulcahy's initial analysis failed to reveal such a clear separation.

According to recent reports, "It wasn't like there's one group of specimens that look bigger than another, and then there's another group that are smaller with smaller horns and canines," he stated. "So I was kind of interested -- are these really good examples of sexual dimorphism after all? Is there actual evidence in the morphology of these skulls, in the distribution in particular of the ranges of morphology we're seeing, that that's what's going on?".

To investigate further, Mulcahy collected additional measurements from fossils housed at other institutions and expanded his analysis using new statistical methods. His final dataset encompassed approximately 30 skulls belonging to a single extinct species, Uintatherium anceps.

Sources indicate that although the results offered some hints of physical differences between the sexes, the evidence was far less convincing than expected. One major challenge in studying extinct animals is that researchers generally cannot independently determine the sex of individual fossil specimens.

Sources indicate that "Maybe there were some little signals of dimorphism here and there, but nothing really concrete," he said. "I had an idea: Maybe it's just that the techniques I'm using aren't robust enough to actually measure sexual dimorphism. With fossil animals, you don't actually know which specimens are males and which are females. You can guess and then test whether or not the ones you guess are males differ from the ones you guess are females, but that's super circular, because you could just be picking the most extreme ones to be one sex and the least extreme to be the other. Of course they're going to differ.".

Modern Bison Provide an Important Comparison.

To determine whether his statistical methods could reliably detect sexual dimorphism, Mulcahy turned to a living mammal: the bison. Unlike fossil uintatheres, modern bison specimens could be classified by sex with confidence.

Bison also offered a useful comparison because they are large, horned herbivores whose ecology shares similarities with what researchers have proposed for uintatheres.

"When you're dealing with living animals, you can just take the males, take the females and compare them," he mentioned. "Bison are another really substantial herbivore, with a similar sort of ecology that's been proposed for uintatheres, and they also have big horns. What I noticed is that the signals of dimorphism I was picking up in bison were a lot clearer. When I was looking at the bison, it was almost perfect that all of the females were most similar to the females, and all the males were most similar to the males.".

Sources indicate that the contrast suggests that the relatively weak evidence for sexual dimorphism in uintatheres cannot be attributed solely to limitations of the statistical techniques. The same methods successfully identified much clearer physical differences between male and female bison.

Victorian-Era Bias May Have Shaped Paleontology.

Mulcahy believes that historical cultural attitudes may help explain why paleontologists came to accept such pronounced differences between male and female uintatheres. Many extinct species were first identified and described during the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when prevailing views about the sexes may have influenced scientific interpretations.

Recent findings suggest that "Back then, this is right when evolutionary theory, sexual selection, natural selection, all of that is kind of coming into play," he said. "I think it's really crucial to remember that these things were first discovered in the late 1800s by a bunch of male paleontologists working in a very Victorian-era mindset. The idea is basically assumed at that point that males are going to be bigger and scarier than females. It's really interesting: When you step back and actually test that hypothesis, it doesn't really hold up.".

Sources indicate that because uintatheres have long been regarded as one of the clearest examples of sexual dimorphism in the fossil record, the newly introduced findings could have implications beyond these unusual prehistoric giants. Other extinct species may also have exhibited less pronounced physical differences between males and females than scientists have traditionally believed.

Rethinking the Evolution of Sex Differences in Mammals.

Recent findings suggest that the research also adds to a growing body of evidence challenging the widespread assumption that male mammals are typically larger than females. Dramatic differences in body size and physical appearance may have evolved independently in multiple mammalian lineages rather than being a characteristic inherited from their earliest common ancestors.

Research on living mammals has similarly challenged conventional thinking, suggesting that pronounced differences favoring larger males are less widespread than historically assumed.

"Strong, big male-style sexual dimorphism was probably not ancestral at the root of the mammalian tree, and among the mammals where we do see this pattern today, it's almost certainly shown up independently several times," Mulcahy said. "It had long been assumed that sexual dimorphism is the norm, that most species show that males are bigger than females. But just a couple years ago, a paper came out showing that among living mammals, most species either don't show any dimorphism or actually have larger females. The idea that males are always bigger than females is really just a choice of what animals were people looking at, what are the things that biologists in the past were interested in.".

Britain's pound is beating every other major currency this year

📅 04 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 3 min read (520 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the British pound crashed to a record low last fall as investors rebelled against budget plans by former Prime Minister Liz Truss.
  • Sterling hit its highest level against the US dollar in 10 months on Tuesday, topping $1.25 for the first time since June 2022.
  • The UK currency has been boosted by indications the country’s economy is holding up better than expected.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the British pound crashed to a record low last fall as investors rebelled against budget plans by former Prime Minister Liz Truss. Now, it’s enjoying a comeback.

Sterling hit its highest level against the US dollar in 10 months on Tuesday, topping $1.25 for the first time since June 2022. The pound, which has advanced about 3.3% versus the greenback since the start of 2023, is the best-performing currency among developed economies this year.

The UK currency has been boosted by indications the country’s economy is holding up better than expected. Activity is now thought to have expanded 0.1% in the final three months of last year, up from a previous estimate of no growth at all. Gross domestic product growth in January has been estimated at 0.3% after dropping 0.5% in December.

According to recent reports, this resilience is bolstering expectations the Bank of England will maintain aggressive interest rate hikes despite concerns about the health of the global banking sector. Rising rates can boost the domestic currency because they help attract foreign investors searching for higher returns.

Inflation in the United Kingdom also jumped to an annual rate of 10.4% in February, underscoring the need for the Bank of England to maintain its tough approach.

The pound plunged close to $1.03 in September 2022 after the Truss government unveiled aims to boost borrowing while slashing taxes, unleashing panic in financial markets that fueled fears of a recession in the United Kingdom.

The International Monetary Fund predicted in January that the UK economy would contract by 0.6% this year, while all other advanced economies would grow, if only slightly.

“There was a lot of pessimism being priced into the pound,” mentioned Francesco Pesole, a currency strategist at ING.

But the sharp pullback in energy prices and China’s reopening have provided some relief about the economic outlook since the start of the year.

“There was a big re-rating of growth expectations around Europe, and that impacted the UK,” Pesole stated.

The euro has also been lifted by these dynamics, rising 2.3% against the US dollar in 2023. The pound’s rally has been sharper in large part because its 2022 declines were more severe, according to Pesole.

Both currencies have been aided by the greenback’s sharp drop from highs reached last September as recession fears have percolated in the United States.

A lack of clarity around the Federal Reserve’s next steps has also restrained the dollar in recent weeks. Investor speculation has increased that the Fed could pause or stop rate hikes due to concerns about the economy following the failure of Silicon Valley Bank last month.

Sources indicate that jordan Rochester, a currency strategist at Nomura, said he thinks the pound could rise to $1.30 this year and “potentially higher.” But he still sees risks given the uncertainty surrounding the Bank of England’s plans and how rate rises will feed back through the country’s economy. And Pesole cautioned that currency fluctuations are often overdone when markets are choppy, as they are now.

“In a volatile market environment, moves are exacerbated,” he said.

#151730. German Catholic Church: Abuse victims may receive higher compensation

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1304 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

German Catholic Church: Abuse victims may receive higher compensation

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1304 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Higher Regional Court of Cologne ruled on Thursday that the Archdiocese of Cologne must pay €550,000 ($603,341) to a now 60-year-old woman.
  • This ruling could result in the Catholic Church paying significantly higher compensation to victims of abuse and sexual violence by priests.
  • The settlement far exceeds previous sums granted in similar cases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Higher Regional Court of Cologne ruled on Thursday that the Archdiocese of Cologne must pay €550,000 ($603,341) to a now 60-year-old woman. Melanie F.*, the claimant, was subjected to serious sexual abuse by a priest in the late 1970s and early 1980s.

This ruling could result in the Catholic Church paying significantly higher compensation to victims of abuse and sexual violence by priests.

The settlement far exceeds previous sums granted in similar cases. Before this, the highest financial compensation awarded by a court was €300,000. This amount was granted by the Regional Court of Cologne in June 2023 to a former altar boy who was abused by a priest for several years.

Melanie F. was represented by the same lawyer. Since she had already received €360,000 in compensation during previous proceedings, the court granted Melanie F. an additional €190,000.

It has been revealed that in determining the appropriate amount of damages, the Seventh Civil Senate of the Higher Regional Court of Cologne pointed to an "abortion performed without the knowledge or consent of the plaintiff, who was only 15 years old at the time" as one of the deciding factors. The judges stated that this incident in particular warranted a substantial increase in compensatory damages. The teenager reportedly became pregnant twice during the period of abuse.

Sources indicate that born in 1966, Melanie F. lived in a Catholic orphanage in Bonn in the late 1970s. Bernd U., then a theology student, worked there as a volunteer and cared for several children. After he was ordained as a priest, he took Melanie and a boy two years her senior from the orphanage to live with him.

Beginning in 1979, he subjected the underage Melanie to severe sexual abuse in his residence at the parish. He threatened to send her back to the orphanage if she refused to comply. He subsequently became the legal guardian of both children. Cardinal Joseph Höffner, who was then the Archbishop of Cologne, approved the arrangement.

Sources indicate that in its written opinion, the court addressed the question of whether an archdiocese can be held liable for the criminal acts of a member of the clergy. The judges decided to overrule the Cologne Regional Court's ruling from 2023 and gave a detailed explanation of their reasoning. Ultimately, they found that the Church was liable under the principles of official liability.

The Regional Court had previously rejected this argument in 2023, siding with the lawyers of the Archdiocese of Cologne. At the time, the judges ruled that the abuse was not sufficiently linked to Bernd U.'s role as a priest. According to the judges, he had abused his foster child in his capacity as a caregiver, not as part of his priestly duties.

Recent findings suggest that the 2023 ruling was met with disbelief and anger within the Archdiocese of Cologne. The archdiocese was already in turmoil because many Catholics were unhappy with how Cardinal Rainer Maria Woelki handled abuse cases. For decades, Church teachings and statements by Cologne's archbishops had repeatedly emphasized that a priest is a priest in all that he does and cannot simply set that role aside.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

But now, the Higher Regional Court of Cologne has concluded that there is in fact a clear connection between Bernd U.'s work for the church and the crimes he committed.

In their decision, they explained that he had assumed a pastoral role in caring for Melanie F. while she was still living in the orphanage and gained her trust through displays of great affection.

Industry observers note that his role at the church was described explicitly by the judges as a "cover." It was only much later that he sought to become the children's foster father, a position he would likely not have been able to obtain so easily without the "cover" of being a celibate Catholic priest. In addition, most of the abuse took place in the rectory.

After the ruling, Melanie F. said she was relieved that her years-long legal battle had finally come to an end. But she said she would never be able to put the abuse behind her. "You can't just block it out; you live with it.".

The Archdiocese of Cologne said it "respectfully" took note of the decision.

In a recent development, the perpetrator, now 74 years old, was sentenced to 12 years in prison at his 2022 trial. The court found that he had abused nine girls, the youngest of whom was nine years old. The Church subsequently removed him from the priesthood.

According to recent reports, "The strategy of the Archdiocese of Cologne to portray its priests' serious sexual crimes as the actions of private individuals has failed miserably," Thomas Schüller, a Catholic canon lawyer, told DW. Schüller described the archdiocese's approach as a "cynical attempt" that betrays the Catholic Church's own understanding of the priestly office.

From now on, the church will be held liable if a priest uses his position to sexually abuse children or teenagers and if the diocese or Protestant regional church has failed to fulfill its supervisory duties adequately.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Recent findings suggest that schüller said that Germany's Catholic bishops must "significantly increase" compensation payments to survivors. Until now, the bishops had consistently argued that the amounts should be based on current court rulings and legal standards.

However, this ruling will now have "significant financial consequences for both churches," he said, describing the ruling as "a day of hope for many survivors of sexual abuse in both churches.".

Matthias Katsch, spokesperson for the survivor advocacy group Eckiger Tisch, also called the ruling "good news.".

"Today, it was made clear that the Church must pay for the harm caused by its officials," he noted. However, he added that the amount was still too low given the horrific nature of the crimes and their lifelong consequences.

Recent findings suggest that "The Archdiocese of Cologne's leadership turned a blind eye or acted with the grossest negligence," he said, allowing the crimes to happen. Melanie F. had sought compensation of between €800,000 and €900,000.

Sources indicate that in March 2026, the Independent Commission for Recognition Payments (UKA), which was established by the German Bishops' Conference in 2021, confirmed that it had approved payments totaling approximately €93 million for survivors in all dioceses. Since then, several dioceses have published additional studies containing new reports of abuse cases.

Sixteen years after survivors and Jesuit priest Klaus Mertes helped bring the abuse scandal to light, the German Bishops' Conference will now have to prepare for significantly higher compensation payments.

In the United States, where civil lawsuits seeking compensation often involve far higher sums than in Germany, a number of Catholic dioceses have filed for bankruptcy. But that is unlikely to happen in Germany. The Bonn-based law firm of Eberhard Luetjohann, Melanie F.'s attorney, has reported receiving inquiries from hundreds of abuse survivors seeking higher compensation.

Spokesperson for Eckiger Tisch, Matthias Katsch, called on church leaders to engage in dialogue with survivors and their advocacy groups. Katsch said the question of the Church's liability for crimes committed by priests lies at the heart of most cases in which survivors are dissatisfied with the Independent Commission for Recognition Payments' decisions and believe they are entitled to higher compensation.

It is unacceptable, he said, that these survivors must go to court to obtain the compensation they deserve.

This article was originally written in German.

*Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspected criminals or victims and urges us to refrain from revealing full names in such cases.

Retail turnarounds are taking hold just in time for the holiday season

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (578 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Once-struggling retailers are entering the holiday quarter with improved performance and sales momentum as turnaround efforts begin to resonate with shoppers.
  • A handful of earnings reports on Tuesday pointed to a mix of factors behind the strong results, including a resilient consumer, stronger execution and demand for the right products at the right price.
  • Industry observers note that kohl's reported comparable sales growth of 1.2% for the period ended Oct.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Once-struggling retailers are entering the holiday quarter with improved performance and sales momentum as turnaround efforts begin to resonate with shoppers.

A handful of earnings reports on Tuesday pointed to a mix of factors behind the strong results, including a resilient consumer, stronger execution and demand for the right products at the right price.

Industry observers note that kohl's reported comparable sales growth of 1.2% for the period ended Oct. 31 and raised its full-year outlook as CEO Michael Bender stated customers "have remained resilient" but are "migrating to value with their purchases.".

He tied improvement to the company's work on product assortment, store experience and value.

Best Buy also on Tuesday posted its highest comparable sales growth in five years, at 6.1%, which prompted the electronics retailer to raise its full-year outlook.

Recent findings suggest that "We have a tremendous amount of momentum," CEO Jason Bonfig told CNBC in an interview. "The fact that we saw pretty much broad-based growth across almost all of our categories is a lot of momentum that we're very excited about.".

The company also credited execution, market share gains and a compelling product cycle alongside growing customer demand.

Recent findings suggest that at Dick's Sporting Goods, quarterly comparable sales rose 2.6% at the core business and 0.5% at Foot Locker. CEO Lauren Hobart stated "all income demographics grew" and the organization "didn't see trade-down from best to better or better to good.".

She similarly pointed to newly introduced products and market share gains within the category as contributing to the strong quarter. She also highlighted continued improvement at Foot Locker.

All three companies have been undergoing efforts to boost sales and get the right products on shelves to meet customer demand.

Target, likewise undergoing revitalization efforts, last week reported comparable sales growth of 5.6% in the third quarter, fueled by a 5% increase in comparable traffic. The retailer raised its full-year outlook.

CEO Michael Fiddelke at the time called the traffic gain "a healthy sign that guests are responding to our changes and choosing Target more often.".

Even Gap CEO Richard Dickson told CNBC the organization has moved from "rebuild mode" to "turnaround mode" at its Old Navy banner, a sign of progress, albeit not a broad-based portfolio recovery.

Michael Baker, a retail analyst at D.A. Davidson, told CNBC he sees both a resilient consumer and company-specific improvements as driving sector strength.

"Retail sales have been more resilient than most think," Baker said. His analysis highlighted retail sales, excluding autos and gas, rose 5.1% in the third quarter on a nonseasonally adjusted basis — the strongest quarter since the pandemic.

But he cautioned that growth appears to be coming more from transaction size than traffic, with inflation, promotions and higher units per transaction driving up spend.

Dollar Tree, which reported better-than-expected earnings on Tuesday morning, posted a 3.8% increase to traffic, accelerating from 0.4% growth in the prior quarter, suggesting more shoppers may be bargain hunting. Comparable sales at the retailer increased 4.6% during the period.

"Consumers are under pressure, and they are increasingly selective about where and how they spend," noted Dollar Tree CEO Michael Creedon on the company's earnings call. "When under pressure, shoppers prioritize value and buy closer to need.".

Comparable sales of everyday essentials rose 8.9% at Dollar Tree stores in the third quarter, while sales of nonessential items were essentially flat, the tech giant said.

— CNBC's Laya Neelakandan contributed to this report.

Industry News: Scientists identify two ages when children may be most vulnerable to screen time

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (979 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that screen time at certain ages may be more closely tied to children's future learning and memory than previously recognized.
  • The findings suggest that when children use screens may be just as important as how much time they spend in front of them.
  • As digital devices become an increasingly common part of childhood, understanding their potential long-term effects has become a growing priority.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that screen time at certain ages may be more closely tied to children's future learning and memory than previously recognized. A new study tracking children from age 1 to 8 found that those who spent more time watching screens during infancy and around the start of elementary school tended to perform worse academically at age 9 and have weaker working memory at age 10.5.

The findings suggest that when children use screens may be just as important as how much time they spend in front of them. Two ages in particular, 1 and 6, emerged as potentially sensitive periods in childhood development.

As digital devices become an increasingly common part of childhood, understanding their potential long-term effects has become a growing priority. Recommendations from the World Health Organization (WHO) and the American Academy of Pediatrics generally emphasize avoiding screen exposure during the first 18 to 24 months of life and limiting it to less than one hour a day for children ages 2 to 5. However, many young children spend considerably more time using screens.

Tracking Screen Time Throughout Childhood.

Despite growing concerns about children's digital habits, previous research has produced mixed findings about the relationship between screen time and cognitive development. Many earlier studies examined children at a single point in time, concentrated on children already attending school, or did not regularly track screen habits throughout early childhood.

Following the same children over several years allows researchers to investigate whether screen exposure at particular ages is more strongly associated with later outcomes. This approach can also help researchers better account for the influence of family circumstances and environmental factors.

In a recent development, scientists from Inserm and the National University of Singapore addressed these gaps in a study published in the World Journal of Pediatrics. The researchers examined data from 502 children participating in the Growing Up in Singapore Towards healthy Outcomes (GUSTO) birth cohort.

Sources indicate that parents reported their children's screen viewing habits at six different points between infancy and middle childhood. The researchers then evaluated the children's academic achievement and working memory several years later.

Working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and manipulate information. It plays an essential role in everyday learning, allowing children to follow instructions, solve math problems, understand sentences, and keep track of information while completing tasks.

Two Ages Stand Out for Screen Time Risks.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers found that greater screen exposure at certain stages of childhood was associated with lower academic achievement and poorer working memory later in life. These relationships were particularly consistent among children who spent more time watching screens at age 1 and around age 6, when formal schooling typically begins.

Recent findings suggest that children who accumulated more screen time throughout childhood also tended to achieve lower academic scores. However, the strength of the associations varied depending on when the exposure occurred, suggesting that some developmental stages may be more sensitive than others.

It has been revealed that one possible explanation is that screen viewing can take time away from activities that support cognitive development, including conversations with caregivers, imaginative play, and hands-on exploration of the physical world. These experiences provide opportunities for children to develop language, attention, memory, and problem-solving skills.

According to recent reports, "The effect sizes we saw at age 1 were the largest among all time points we examined," the authors said. "That suggests early infancy may be a window of heightened sensitivity, when the developing brain is particularly vulnerable to the displacement of learning interactions by screen time. We were also surprised to see that while screen use at age 2 and 3 did not show significant links, the associations re-emerged at age 6 -- when children enter formal schooling. So it is not just about early years; screen use later in childhood still matters.".

Although the study identifies associations rather than proving that screen time directly causes poorer cognitive or academic outcomes, the results highlight the potential importance of managing children's screen habits at different ages.

Why Even Small Differences in Screen Time Matter.

According to the researchers, the results reinforce the principle that "less is better" when it comes to children's screen time.

An additional hour of daily screen viewing may not produce a noticeable difference in an individual child's academic abilities. However, when similar patterns occur across a large population, even relatively small differences in average performance could increase the number of children who experience academic difficulties.

It has been revealed that the researchers suggest that efforts to encourage healthier screen habits could begin during infancy, with renewed emphasis around the transition to elementary school. This approach recognizes that children's developmental needs continue to change well beyond their toddler years.

The authors also stress that the amount of time children spend in front of screens is only one part of a much larger picture. Future studies should investigate whether the quality of digital content, the types of devices children use, and whether parents watch and interact with their children during screen time influence developmental outcomes.

Understanding these differences could eventually help researchers develop more targeted recommendations that consider not only how much screen time children get, but also when and how they engage with digital technology.

According to recent reports, the GUSTO study was supported by the Singapore National Research Foundation and the Singapore Ministry of Health's National Medical Research Council (NMRC/TCR/004-NUS/2008 and NMRC/TCR/012-NUHS/2014). Additional funding came from the Agence Nationale de la Recherche (ANR) in France (iSCAN project, ANR-20-CE36-0001).

#151718. Latest Update: Scientists turn one of the world’s hardest-to-recycle plastics into high-performance lubricating oil

📖 Baca

Latest Update: Scientists turn one of the world’s hardest-to-recycle plastics into high-performance lubricating oil

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1131 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Old plumbing pipes, discarded window frames, and expired credit cards could one day become valuable ingredients in engine oil.
  • Led by chemist and chemical engineer Guoliang "Greg" Liu, the research team discovered how to convert polyvinyl chloride (PVC) into polyalphaolefin, a key ingredient in synthetic lubricants such as engine oil.
  • Published in the journal Nature, the research offers a potential solution to two environmental challenges: reducing the accumulation of stubborn plastic waste and finding more sustainable ways to manufacture valuable industrial lubricants.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Old plumbing pipes, discarded window frames, and expired credit cards could one day become valuable ingredients in engine oil. Researchers at Virginia Tech have developed a newly introduced chemical process that transforms one of the world's most difficult plastics to recycle into a high-performance lubricant material.

Led by chemist and chemical engineer Guoliang "Greg" Liu, the research team discovered how to convert polyvinyl chloride (PVC) into polyalphaolefin, a key ingredient in synthetic lubricants such as engine oil.

Published in the journal Nature, the research offers a potential solution to two environmental challenges: reducing the accumulation of stubborn plastic waste and finding more sustainable ways to manufacture valuable industrial lubricants.

PVC is particularly difficult to recycle because of its chlorine content and the wide range of chemical additives manufacturers incorporate into their products. These additives can give PVC different properties, such as flexibility, rigidity, and resistance to heat. However, they also complicate conventional recycling methods. Consequently, much of the world's discarded PVC ends up in landfills.

Turning Plastic Waste Into High-Performance Lubricants.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, global demand for lubricants continues to grow, and producing these materials can come with significant environmental costs. Transforming discarded PVC into a valuable lubricant ingredient could help address both problems.

Although lubricants rarely attract much attention, they are essential to modern machinery. They reduce friction and wear between moving components, helping engines operate efficiently and extending the lifespan of mechanical equipment. Everything from lawn mowers and passenger vehicles to jet engines depends on reliable lubricants.

The Virginia Tech team's process could provide an alternative source of these vital materials while helping address the growing problem of plastic pollution.

Industry observers note that to make the lubricant, researchers place PVC of the kind commonly used in household plumbing, window frames, and credit cards into a solvent. They then introduce aluminum trichloride and alpha-olefins, a class of hydrocarbons used in the manufacture of synthetic lubricants. The mixture is heated to 158 degrees Fahrenheit for three hours, after which the researchers extract a relatively thick lubricating oil.

Industry observers note that the resulting polyalphaolefin belongs to a family of synthetic base oils valued for their stability, lubricating properties, and ability to perform across a wide range of temperatures. These materials are commonly used as the foundation for high-performance synthetic engine oils.

In a recent development, "Number one, we have proved that it is feasible to use plastic waste to make high-performance lubricants. Number two, these lubricants are green, and they can meet the emerging needs for sustainability by the market," Liu mentioned.

Building on Earlier Plastic Recycling Breakthroughs.

The discovery grew out of previous research by Liu's laboratory, published in Science and Nature Sustainability. In those studies, the researchers demonstrated how other types of plastic waste could be transformed into surfactants, substances that help water interact with oils and grease and are widely used in soaps and detergents.

Encouraged by those successes, the researchers decided to tackle the more challenging problem of PVC waste.

"We want to help improve the recycling and upcycling of PVC," Liu remarked.

Unlike conventional recycling, which typically aims to recover materials for reuse, upcycling seeks to transform discarded materials into products with greater value or usefulness.

In a recent development, liu recruited a group of graduate researchers to investigate this possibility. Eric Munyaneza Nuwayo, who was completing the final year of his doctoral program, was selected to lead the project. Connor S. Thompson, a chemistry graduate student who had been pursuing a different research topic, joined the effort after Liu suggested changing direction.

Abby Civiello, a graduate student in her first year, also joined the team and quickly became an vital contributor to the research.

"I often called them the three musketeers," Liu mentioned.

An Unexpected Discovery in Polymer Chemistry.

The researchers initially experimented with ways to modify the molecular structure of PVC and convert it into more useful substances.

Like other plastics, PVC is a polymer, meaning it consists of long molecular chains made up of repeating chemical units. The researchers initially hoped that changing the chemical groups attached to these chains would produce a material with desirable properties.

"The idea was simple. PVC, as one of the most activated forms of polyethylene, ought to be easily converted into some other molecules by replacing the chlorine atoms with other groups," Liu noted.

However, the early experiments consistently produced disappointing results. Instead of creating a functional material with the desired performance characteristics, the team ended up with soft, sticky substances that had little practical value.

Those frustrating results eventually inspired Liu to approach the problem differently. Rather than continuing to modify the long molecular chains, he wondered whether breaking them into smaller pieces might produce something more useful.

"One day I realized -- if this polymer is so gooey and so soft, why don't I just keep breaking the polymer chains down to smaller segments?" said Liu.

As the researchers refined their chemical process and evaluated the properties of the materials it produced, Liu began to recognize that the team had discovered something with implications extending well beyond plastic recycling.

They had found a potential fresh route for manufacturing valuable industrial lubricants.

Bringing Recycled Plastic Lubricants to the Market.

To better understand the properties and commercial potential of the fresh oil, Liu enlisted the expertise of researchers at several institutions.

He provided samples to Ali Erdemir at Texas A&M University, where researchers evaluated the performance of the finished materials. William Goddard at the California Institute of Technology, or Caltech, contributed chemical computations to help investigate the underlying chemistry.

At Virginia Tech, Xi Chen examined the economic and manufacturing aspects of the technology, developing models to explore how the oil could be produced on a larger scale.

It has been revealed that the research establishes that discarded PVC can serve as a starting material for producing high-performance lubricants. However, expanding the process beyond the laboratory remains an important next step.

Liu hopes to further improve the environmental sustainability of the technology while making the resulting lubricants more widely available. Ultimately, the approach could give one of the world's most problematic plastics a valuable second life and provide industries with an alternative source of essential lubricating materials.

"Lubricants are the silent hero out there. We often don't recognize they exist, but they are out there working quietly. We want to be able to produce the oil on a larger scale to reach more people in the world," Liu said.

#151713. The narwhal’s legendary “unicorn horn” holds a remarkable engineering secret

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1357 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

The narwhal’s legendary “unicorn horn” holds a remarkable engineering secret

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1357 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the 17th century, Danish King Frederik III already knew that the legendary unicorn horn came from a real animal.
  • Industry observers note that the narwhal's tusk is unlike almost any other tooth in nature.
  • This unusual biological structure caught the attention of an international team of researchers from several scientific disciplines.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the 17th century, Danish King Frederik III already knew that the legendary unicorn horn came from a real animal. However, this creature had fins instead of hooves and inhabited the icy waters of the Arctic. The king dispatched an expedition to Greenland to investigate the source of these highly prized objects. The successful mission earned him a throne fashioned entirely from "unicorn horns," enhancing his power and prestige across Europe. Yet the treasured horn was not actually a horn, but "merely" a tooth.

Industry observers note that the narwhal's tusk is unlike almost any other tooth in nature. Whereas elongated teeth, including elephant and walrus tusks and beaver incisors, grow in curved shapes, the male narwhal develops a remarkable corkscrew-shaped tooth. Typically, the upper left canine grows forward through the upper lip, twisting counterclockwise as it extends. It can reach two meters (6.6 feet) in length, equivalent to as much as half the animal's body length.

This unusual biological structure caught the attention of an international team of researchers from several scientific disciplines. Using advanced X-ray imaging techniques, they set out to determine whether the arrangement of the tusk's microscopic building blocks could explain the direction of its visible spiral.

What they discovered was even more remarkable than expected. Rather than forming a single spiral, the tusk's tiny structural components create two intertwined helices that twist in opposite directions. Together, they produce an exceptionally stable structure.

According to recent reports, the research was conducted at three major European synchrotron facilities: the Swiss Light Source SLS at the Paul Scherrer Institute in Villigen, the MAX IV Laboratory in Lund (Sweden), and the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility ESRF in Grenoble (France). The findings were published in Nature Communications.

A Giant Tooth Built Like Reinforced Concrete.

Recent findings suggest that narwhal tusks continue growing throughout the animals' lives and can easily reach 70 years of age. Despite their striking appearance, the precise purpose of these enormous teeth remains uncertain. Evidence suggests they are primarily involved in mate selection. Narwhals have also been observed crossing their tusks in playful "duels," supporting the idea that the structures are key for reproduction and social interactions.

Although questions remain about how narwhals use their tusks, scientists now have a much clearer picture of how they are constructed.

"Like bones or other teeth in the animal kingdom, the narwhal tusk is a complex composite material whose structure extends from tiny nanoscale building blocks to the visible form of the entire tooth," says Marianne Liebi, a PSI researcher and co-author of the study.

In a recent development, composite materials combine different substances to achieve properties that the individual components cannot provide alone. Reinforced concrete is a familiar example. Concrete made from cement and sand can withstand considerable pressure, while an internal steel framework helps resist pulling forces and provides additional stability.

It has been revealed that "The narwhal tusk, too, must be both hard and flexible," Liebi explains. "Only then can it withstand the strong hydrodynamic forces that swimming generates.".

The Remarkable Microscopic Structure of Narwhal Tusks.

Sources indicate that most of the narwhal's tusk consists of dentin, the same hard tissue that makes up much of the interior of human teeth. A thinner layer of cementum covers its exterior. In other mammals, cementum is typically confined to the roots of teeth.

It has been revealed that both materials contain extremely fine collagen fibers strengthened by tiny mineral crystals. Much like the steel framework inside reinforced concrete, the collagen fibers provide internal reinforcement, while the mineral crystals supply hardness. This combination allows the tusk to possess both strength and flexibility.

Understanding how this microscopic arrangement produces the much larger spiral presented a significant scientific challenge.

"The collagen fibers and mineral crystals are on the nanometer scale, while the spiral of the tooth only becomes visible at centimeter and meter lengths," Marianne Liebi explains.

Sources indicate that A nanometer is one billionth of a meter. To investigate how structures at this incredibly small scale relate to the shape of an entire tusk, the researchers turned to a sophisticated X-ray imaging method known as tensor tomography.

Advanced X-Rays Reveal the Tusk's Hidden Architecture.

Conventional dental X-rays produce images because teeth absorb more radiation than the softer tissues around them. The resulting image is essentially a shadow that reveals the shape and density of the tooth.

However, the powerful X-rays generated at synchrotron research facilities can provide far more detailed information. When these beams encounter regularly organized structures inside a material, the X-rays scatter in distinctive patterns. Scientists can analyze those patterns to determine how microscopic components are arranged.

"From these patterns, we can calculate how the nanometer-sized mineralized collagen fibers inside the material are oriented," explains first author Adrian Rodriguez-Palomo.

Industry observers note that rodriguez-Palomo began working on the project while pursuing his PhD at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden. He subsequently continued the research as a postdoctoral researcher at Aarhus University in Denmark.

During tensor tomography, researchers rotate the tooth within the synchrotron's X-ray beam while collecting measurements at individual locations. Millions of these measurements are then combined to reconstruct a three-dimensional representation of the tusk's internal organization, connecting its microscopic components with the much larger structure.

An Unexpected Discovery Hidden in the Data.

When the researchers first examined their extensive imaging data, they could not find the spiral structure they had anticipated.

"That puzzled us quite a bit," recalls Marianne Liebi.

Earlier mechanical experiments had indicated that the tusk's characteristic twist should be reflected in the orientation of its collagen fibers and mineral crystals.

"But instead of a helix, all we saw was a regular pattern.".

Industry observers note that the breakthrough came when the scientists changed their approach. Rather than examining individual points in the three-dimensional images in isolation, they investigated how the orientation of each point related to its neighbors.

In a recent development, "When we compared how these points were oriented relative to each other, a directional trend began to appear," recalls Palomo. "All we had to do then was connect the dots - as in a children's paint-by-numbers kit - and suddenly the structure became visible: two intertwined spirals.".

Two Opposing Spirals Give Narwhal Tusks Their Strength.

Further examination revealed that the two spirals occupy different regions of the tooth. The thin outer cementum layer forms a left-handed helix, whereas the mineralized collagen structures within the underlying dentin spiral in the opposite direction.

This sophisticated natural design provides substantial mechanical advantages. Much like the intertwined strands of a rope, the two opposing helices work together to create an exceptionally stable structure. Their arrangement helps the tusk resist twisting forces, known as torsion, as well as other forms of mechanical stress.

The same microscopic architecture also produces the narwhal's recognizable corkscrew shape, linking the extraordinary appearance of the legendary unicorn horn to structures far too small to see with the naked eye.

Narwhal Tusks Preserve Decades of Arctic History.

The study forms part of a research project funded by NordForsk called "Narwhal tusks - a tale with a twist." It also received support from the European Union's Horizon 2020 research and innovation program under the Marie Skłodowska-Curie program.

Under the leadership of Henrik Birkedal of Aarhus University in Denmark, the international and interdisciplinary research team is exploring both the internal architecture of narwhal tusks and the relationship between tusk growth, environmental conditions, and climate.

As a narwhal's tusk grows, it develops successive layers that function much like the annual growth rings of a tree. Scientists can examine these structures to reconstruct past Arctic environmental conditions, including changes in climate and food availability.

During a lifespan that can approach a century, a male narwhal effectively builds its own environmental archive within its remarkable spiral tooth.

#151712. Secondhand shopping is going mainstream this holiday season as consumers seek value

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1012 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

Secondhand shopping is going mainstream this holiday season as consumers seek value

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1012 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As the high cost of living squeezes consumers' wallets this holiday season, more shoppers are turning to secondhand retail and thrifting.
  • Recent findings suggest that the shift comes as consumers look for better value, buyers put more emphasis on personalization and younger generations change the way they shop.
  • It has been revealed that that segment is expected to reach nearly $80 billion by 2030, growing more than 7% annually on average, GlobalData found.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the high cost of living squeezes consumers' wallets this holiday season, more shoppers are turning to secondhand retail and thrifting.

Recent findings suggest that the shift comes as consumers look for better value, buyers put more emphasis on personalization and younger generations change the way they shop. The U.S. secondhand apparel market grew 13% in 2025, nearly four times faster than the overall retail clothing market, according to GlobalData.

It has been revealed that that segment is expected to reach nearly $80 billion by 2030, growing more than 7% annually on average, GlobalData found. Much of that expansion — 40% — was driven by Generation Z, followed closely by millennials.

"I think this has been their version of the thrill of the hunt that millennials loved during the recession days," Katherine Cullen, a global senior retail analyst at EY, told CNBC. "It's a way to really express an individual style, find something unique, something that really fits their own vibe and personality.".

It goes beyond people shopping for themselves, Cullen said. With more emphasis on unique holiday gifts, shoppers are leaning more on secondhand retail than they have before, whether in clothing or in other retail categories.

They're looking for something that fits the personality of the person they're shopping for, she added.

It has been revealed that for Vanessa Roberts, that meant finding two antique children's chairs that she says will perfectly round out her nieces' play space. Roberts, 37, said she's been thrifting for at least two decades, each time embracing the "thrill" of finding something unique or vintage.

Especially in fashion, at a time when the quality of mass-produced items has decreased, thrifted items offer more value beyond just the price tag, Roberts added.

"It's crazy that you can find better quality items at the thrift store right now from 20 years ago versus what you can find at stores right now," she noted.

According to recent reports, roberts, who lives in Los Angeles, said she began shopping for holiday gifts in September. As she prepares her haul for December, roughly 70% of her gifting will come from secondhand stores, she estimated.

According to recent reports, "It's been a fun little challenge, where it's like a little scavenger hunt when I go into the thrift store," she mentioned. "I'm definitely thrifting for the holidays – I do it every year.".

The trend coincides with an economy that has forced consumers to be more intentional about how they spend, as they face high inflation and elevated gas prices.

In October, the consumer price index rose a seasonally adjusted 0.4%, which was more than anticipated. Still, consumers are expected to continue spending through the holiday season, with sales projected to top $1 trillion for the first time — though some of that estimated increase is boosted by inflation.

"You have a consumer who, while they're willing to spend at the top level, they're willing to splurge selectively," Cullen noted. "Consumers are looking for value, which I think is something that is making secondhand resale and re-commerce more attractive.".

And while clothing is largely the entry point to buying resale, secondhand shopping is increasingly expanding into furniture, electronics and books, according to a report from consumer insights firm The Consumer Collective.

Its October report found that 34% of people surveyed remarked secondhand products offer better value than brand new ones.

Many secondhand items also have an inherent added value beyond the low price on the tag, according to eBay CEO Jamie Iannone. The uniqueness of those products, as well as the allure that vintage adds to them, means consumers may actually be seeking the benefits of secondhand in more ways than one.

Sources indicate that "I can buy a product that's used, and it almost has cachet around it," Iannone told CNBC. "Consumers today, they're able to get these amazing values on products, and it's seen as very normal to be gifting pre-loved.".

Sources indicate that according to eBay's Recommerce Report in October, 70% of global consumers surveyed noted they consider secondhand shopping vital for managing their budgets. That same report also found that 89% of respondents proposal to spend the same amount or more on secondhand products next year compared with this year.

Iannone stated he thinks the interest in secondhand this holiday season is "much stronger" than last year.

"It's becoming just a more established part of consumers' shopping and gifting routines," he said.

At a time when algorithms are driving shopping trends, consumers are also looking for ways to distinguish themselves and their purchases.

That's stretching beyond buying for themselves to purchasing holiday gifts for others, too.

In a recent development, "Secondhand is where they're finding unique items to wear," Alon Rotem, chief strategy officer at ThredUp, told CNBC. The company's holiday survey found that respondents valued uniqueness nearly as much as the value of a thrifted piece.

"To me, that represents a pretty meaningful shift in consumer taste," he added.

It's partly why ThredUp, which is an online thrift marketplace, emphasizes that each of its products is "a snowflake," Rotem said — something unique.

That's the appeal of buying preowned, rather than purchasing off the rack that hundreds of other people are reaching for, too.

Industry observers note that "Consumer tastes have changed, and they're much more into vintage," he added. "Uniqueness has a premium in their minds.".

It has been revealed that larger retailers are taking note, EY's Cullen stated. More retailers, such as Lululemon, Patagonia and Madewell, are dabbling in preowned.

Wall Street is also increasingly watching the growing secondhand trend. Though shares of some secondhand and resale companies such as eBay and Savers Value Village have climbed this year, shares of both ThredUp and The RealReal have tumbled year to date.

It has been revealed that "There's a lot of conversation around authenticity or the best find," Cullen remarked. "I think that interest and momentum, along with some of the economic factors that we're all facing, the idea that people are looking to be frugal is going to just continue.".
